historian: b (independent; did not read historian a)
status: EVIDENCE PASS. Proposals for the adjudicator; nothing here is applied to the time model, the site, or data-src/time/time_anchors.json.

time_standard.standard: Local watch time as written by each witness, read as local mean time at Gettysburg (39.83 N, 77.23 W), the standard the time module uses (data-src/time/time_anchors.json, tz "LMT"). 1863 had no time zones; EST would be about +9 minutes. No conversion is applied.
time_standard.scatter: Uncalibrated watches: the same event is stamped 10 to 30 minutes apart by witnesses a few hundred yards apart (examples: Howard 11.15 and 11.30 for one piece of news; Hancock's own 3 p.m. and 5.25 dispatch for his arrival). Windows below include that scatter; none is a precision claim.

method: Official Records vol. 27 parts 1 to 3: the Internet Archive OCR text already in tmp/historian-cache (the same three items listed in historian-src/corpus/or27/manifest.json), searched by regular expression; every quoted string was checked to be present in that text (tmp/clock-hist-b/quotes.py; every quote in this file was asserted present when the file was generated). Pages are the Archive folio from historian-src/corpus/or27/time_claims.json where the corpus has the claim ("cf"), otherwise the printed running head in the OCR ("rh").

Other open texts fetched from the Internet Archive (one request per few seconds, honest User-Agent): Battles and Leaders vol. 3, Southern Historical Society Papers vols. 4, 5, 6, 33, 34, Taylor Four Years with General Lee, Alexander Military Memoirs of a Confederate, Doubleday Chancellorsville and Gettysburg, Report of the Joint Committee on the Conduct of the War (1865), Maine at Gettysburg, Dawes, Howard Autobiography.
NPS pages fetched (overview, Little Round Top; East Cemetery Hill and Pickett's Charge pages gave 404): no clock times; one NPS page transcribes Eshleman's report.
Not used: HathiTrust, Perseus, ehistory.osu.edu (blocked or not tried), any copyright secondary (Pfanz, Coddington, Busey and Hartwig, Desjardin, Gottfried, Sears, Wert, Hessler).
blocked_or_missing: Oates 1905 memoir (Emory scan is not exposed as text), Smith/Campbell Brown/Marshall accounts of the delivery of Lee's message, Sickles's own report, Pickett's report (none exists).

claims.work: Official Records, Series I, vol. 27, pt. 1
claims.page_basis: printed running head in the Internet Archive OCR text
claims.written: date not checked (report of the campaign)

claims.quote: brought the sad tidings of his death

claims.who: Maj. Gen. Carl Schurz (arrived about 11.30 and was told Reynolds "had just been killed")
claims.work: Official Records, Series I, vol. 27, pt. 1
claims.page_basis: Archive folio of the scan leaf, from historian-src/corpus/or27/time_claims.json
claims.claim: Same moment as Howard: on reaching Howard at about 11.30 he is told Reynolds had just been killed.
claims.quote: You informed me that General Reynolds had just been killed

claims.who: Maj. Gen. George G. Meade (report, from Howard's account)
claims.work: Official Records, Series I, vol. 27, pt. 1
claims.page_basis: Archive folio of the scan leaf, from historian-src/corpus/or27/time_claims.json
claims.claim: Puts Howard's arrival after Reynolds fell at "about this time, 11.30 a.m."
claims.quote: who arrived about this time, 11.30 a. m.

claims.who: Abner Doubleday, Chancellorsville and Gettysburg (1882)
claims.work: Chancellorsville and Gettysburg
claims.page_basis: printed running head in the Internet Archive OCR text
claims.claim: Memoir repeats that at 11.30 a.m. Howard learned Reynolds was killed.
claims.quote: At 11.30 a.m he learned that General Reynolds was killed

claims.who: Maj. Gen. Henry Heth (Confederate; not near the spot)
claims.work: Official Records, Series I, vol. 27, pt. 2
claims.page_basis: Archive folio of the scan leaf, from historian-src/corpus/or27/time_claims.json
claims.claim: Gives "9 o'clock" for his own approach and credits a shell of Pegram's with killing Reynolds; the cause is wrong (a rifle bullet), so his clock for the death is not used.
claims.quote: One of the first shells fired by Pegram mortally wounded Major-General Reynolds

anchors.reasoning: Two Union generals who were there or arrived minutes after (Wadsworth, Doubleday) give "about 10.15" for the shot. The sequence evidence (Reynolds put Hall's guns in position, which opened at 10.45; Buford's 10.10 stamp; the news at Howard at 10.45 to 11.30) says the death cannot be much earlier than 10.15 and may be as late as about 10.50. The stated time, not a mean, is kept as the best-supported point; the window shows the later possibility. Howard's 11.15 and 11.30 are the arrival of the news, not the shot, and are upper bounds only.
anchors.corroboration: None independent for the clock figure itself: Doubleday's 10.15 may derive from Wadsworth. Upper bound (11.30) has four separate A1/A2 statements (Howard, Schurz, Meade, Doubleday 1882) that all trace to the same moment. Secondary sources (Pfanz, Busey and Hartwig, Coddington) were not read; no NPS page found carries a clock time for the death.
not_verified: Wadsworth and Doubleday printed text was confirmed against the Internet Archive OCR only, not against the page images.
The 10:40-10:50 figure cited in the older anchor file has no source in this pass; it appears only as the upper edge of the sequence-based window.

claims.page_basis: printed running head in the Internet Archive OCR text

claims.who: Maj. Gen. O. O. Howard (report)
claims.work: Official Records, Series I, vol. 27, pt. 1
claims.page_basis: Archive folio of the scan leaf, from historian-src/corpus/or27/time_claims.json
claims.claim: Order to fall back from the town at 4.10 p.m.; the columns reached Cemetery Hill at 4.30 (same page). The retreat Lee saw begins about here.
claims.quote: At 4.10 p. m., finding that I could hold out no longer

claims.who: Brig. Gen. H. J. Hunt, "The First Day at Gettysburg"
claims.work: Battles and Leaders of the Civil War, vol. 3
claims.page_basis: printed running head in the Internet Archive OCR text
claims.claim: Ewell entered the town about 4:30 pm; Ewell says the message came on entering the town.
claims.quote: Ewell entering the town about 4:30 p.m.

claims.who: Maj. Gen. W. S. Hancock (dispatch stamped 5.25 p.m., July 1)
claims.work: Official Records, Series I, vol. 27, pt. 1
claims.page_basis: printed running head in the Internet Archive OCR text
claims.claim: By 5.25 the Union had a position and "the battle is quiet now"; the confusion Lee's message presupposes is over, so the message was sent before about 17:15 and received before about 17:30.
claims.quote: The battle is quiet now. I think we will be all right until night.

claims.who: Maj. Gen. W. S. Hancock (same dispatch)
claims.work: Official Records, Series I, vol. 27, pt. 1
claims.page_basis: printed running head in the Internet Archive OCR text
claims.claim: He arrived "an hour since", so about 16:25 by his own watch; keeps tick 72 (16:20) in order.
claims.quote: When I arrived here an hour since

anchors.reasoning: No source read here gives a clock time for the message. The window is an inference: the earliest moment is when the Union retreat through the town was visible to Lee and a rider could reach Ewell (retreat order 4.10 pm, Cemetery Hill 4.30 pm, Ewell in the town about 4.30 pm); the latest is Hancock's 5.25 pm dispatch, by which the Union line had formed and the "confusion" of Taylor's message no longer held. That gives 16:30 to 17:30 for the message reaching Ewell. It is not a time reported by anyone, so no point is chosen and the status is UNRESOLVED.
anchors.corroboration: The earlier proposals (17:00, range 16:30-17:30 from a search summary and Stone Sentinels) are consistent with the window but rest on no located primary text. Lee's "if practicable" wording is in his report; Ewell's version ("attack this hill, if I could do so to advantage") differs and is a separate disagreement about the wording, not the time.
not_verified: Capt. James Power Smith and Maj. Campbell Brown (Ewell's staff) and Lt. Col. Charles Marshall are named in the literature as sources for the delivery; their accounts could not be found in open text in this pass.
Heth's, Pender's and Hill's reports were not searched for an indirect clock.

claims.work: Official Records, Series I, vol. 27, pt. 1

claims.who: Maj. Gen. G. G. Meade (report; second-hand)
claims.work: Official Records, Series I, vol. 27, pt. 1
claims.page_basis: printed running head in the Internet Archive OCR text
claims.claim: Slocum and Sickles "reached the ground" about 7 p.m. Meade was at Taneytown; he follows Howard.
claims.quote: About 7 p. m., Major-Generals Slocum and Sickles, with the Twelfth Corps

claims.who: Maj. Gen. O. O. Howard (report)
claims.work: Official Records, Series I, vol. 27, pt. 1
claims.page_basis: printed running head in the Internet Archive OCR text
claims.claim: Slocum and Sickles arrived at the cemetery "about 7 p.m."; Hancock says Sickles's corps was in sight by 5-6, so Howard's figure reads as the time the generals gathered, not the corps arriving.
claims.quote: About 7 p. m. Generals Slocum and Sickles arrived at the cemetery

claims.who: Maj. Gen. Edward Johnson (Confederate; the "Johnson" half of the label)
claims.work: Official Records, Series I, vol. 27, pt. 2
claims.page_basis: printed running head in the Internet Archive OCR text
claims.claim: His division did not arrive in time for the July 1 action and formed line "late on the night of July 1"; Ewell had been told it was close to the town when Lee's message came. No clock time for the arrival.
claims.quote: Late on the night of July 1, I moved along the Gettysburg

anchors.reasoning: Hancock's time-stamped 5.25 p.m. note is the only clock written at the moment, and it says Slocum is coming on the ground then; his report (5-6) and Birney's 5.30 for the Third Corps head agree. Geary's 5 p.m. fits. Howard and Meade say 7 p.m.; both name the generals, not the troops, and Meade follows Howard. The Hancock cluster is chosen (two A1 statements by the officer who handed the command over, plus two cross-checks); 7 p.m. stays in the record as an outlier, not averaged. Johnson cannot be put on a clock: UNRESOLVED for that half (near the town by about 17:30 on Ewell's account; in line only late that night on his own).
anchors.corroboration: Hancock 5.25 note, Hancock report, Geary 5 p.m. and Birney 5.30 are four separate witnesses to a 17:00-17:30 arrival of the XII/III Corps heads.
not_verified: Slocum's own report (p. 759) gives no arrival time.
Johnson's arrival on a clock was not found; the "Johnson" half of the label has no time evidence.
anchors.content_defect_reported: The animation at tick 90 shows all six XII Corps brigades in line on Culp's Hill on the evening of July 1. The sources read here say Geary's division was on the extreme left of the line (the hills south and west of the town) that night and went to Culp's Hill at 5 a.m. on July 2 (Geary p. 825), and Ruger's division moved onto it about 9 a.m. (p. 778). The event is an arrival on the field at about 17:25, not an occupation of Culp's Hill. Report to the data owner; the clock fix does not repair it.

claims.who: Brig. Gen. A. A. Humphreys (Second Division, III Corps)
claims.work: Official Records, Series I, vol. 27, pt. 1
claims.page_basis: Archive folio of the scan leaf, from historian-src/corpus/or27/time_claims.json

claims.who: Brig. Gen. A. A. Humphreys
claims.work: Official Records, Series I, vol. 27, pt. 1
claims.page_basis: Archive folio of the scan leaf, from historian-src/corpus/or27/time_claims.json
claims.claim: About 4 p.m., on Sickles's orders, he moved the division forward to the Emmitsburg Road; the forward line was complete only then.
claims.quote: About 4 p. m. , in compliance with General Sickles’ orders

anchors.reasoning: The sources describe a movement in stages, so two events share the label. The line at the Peach Orchard was being formed about 1 to 2 p.m. (Randolph, Hunt, de Trobriand, Clark p. 585), and the move was seen as an advance by the two officers outside the corps, Hancock and Meade, at about 3 p.m.; Humphreys put the Second Division on the Emmitsburg Road at about 4 p.m. The animation keyframe shows the corps already at the Orchard and on the Emmitsburg Road (Carr, Excelsior), which is the complete state, so the best-supported time for that state is 15:00 within a 14:00 to 16:00 window. If the event is read as the start of the move, the window is 13:00 to 14:00. Both readings are recorded; no mean is taken.
anchors.corroboration: Hancock and Meade, outside the corps, agree on about 3 p.m.; Randolph (1 to 2), de Trobriand and Clark (about 2) inside the corps and Hunt (about 2, on the ground) agree for the forming line. Sickles's Joint Committee testimony (pp. 298-299) has no clock but says he took the line before he was called to the corps commanders' conference, which Sykes (pp. 592-593) puts at 3 p.m.
not_verified: Sickles's own report is not in the Official Records volume read; his testimony gives no clock.
Capt. Clark's "about 2 p.m." is cited from the corpus claim (p. 585); the sentence in the OCR is garbled and is not quoted.
Sykes (p. 592-593) and Warren were not searched for a time of the advance.

anchors.reasoning: No participant gives a clock time for the charge. It follows about an hour of severe fighting that began after the 15th Alabama arrived (Law: his brigade attacked from about 5; Chamberlain: the march began about 4 and the first assault came before his line was complete), and it precedes Fisher's arrival "at dusk" and the 8 p.m. consolidation. Woodward (adjacent) says the attackers fell back "nearly 6 p.m.", and a 1898 secondary says about 6:30. The first-hand statement closest to the event is Woodward, so about 18:00 is chosen; the window reaches 17:30 (an hour after the earliest start) and 18:45. The earlier lower edge of 17:10 has no support here.
anchors.corroboration: Chamberlain, Rice, Woodward and Law are independent of each other. Maine at Gettysburg is secondary and unsourced for its time. Oates (15th Alabama) gives no clock in his report and his 1905 book could not be fetched as open text; Pullen and Desjardin (copyright) were not read.
not_verified: No primary source states a clock time for the charge; the window is an inference from sequence and duration.

Woodward's regiment-clock runs early (2.30 / 3.15) against Chamberlain's 4 p.m. march start, so his "nearly 6" may sit 30 to 60 minutes early on a common clock; this is why the window extends to 18:45.

anchors.reasoning: Lee, Hunt, Harrow and Meade, and the Union recollections generally, put the cannonade at about 1 p.m. and the infantry coming out at about 3 p.m. (about two hours later: Lee "about two hours", Cabell "over two hours", Hunt "about 3"). Alexander's timed notes put the order at 1.25 to 1.40 and the start about 14:00; Peyton's brigade 14:30. Alexander's opening time (1 p.m.) agrees with everyone else's, so a simple watch offset does not explain the gap; his reconstruction of the notes and the wait before the advance runs about an hour shorter than the cannonade length every other witness gives ("about two hours"), and his own two accounts differ by five minutes. The A1 cluster (Lee, Hunt, Harrow) is chosen: 15:00. Alexander's figure stays as the early edge of the window, with the contest recorded. Consistency check (an estimate, not evidence): a mile at quick time with halts takes about 20 to 30 minutes, so a 15:00 start puts the leading brigades at the wall at about 15:20 to 15:30, in line with the 15:35 anchor (tick 551).
anchors.corroboration: Lee (Confederate, official), Hunt and Harrow (Union, official) give independent 15:00 readings; Cabell and Longstreet describe the duration that implies it. NPS pages found carry no clock time (they describe a bombardment of "about two hours" in general terms).
not_verified: The cause of Alexander's earlier chronology was not identified.
Pickett's, Kemper's and Armistead's own reports for the step-off time were not found (Pickett filed none in the OR).
Hays (OR 27/1, brigade report) writes of firing "until 4.30 o'clock"; the page was not verified and he is not listed above.
